Pfizer's filings don't use the name "Cost Realignment Program". The closest match is the "Realigning Our Cost Base Program", and this answer assumes that is the program meant. The latest 10-Q (Q2 2026) says Pfizer now expects total net cost savings of approximately $6.7 billion from the program through 2029. That is up from approximately $5.7 billion through 2026, which the FY2025 10-K had described as $5.1 billion achieved through 2025 plus $600 million still to come. The extra $1.0 billion is expected to be realized from 2027 through 2029. Pfizer expects about $2.0 billion of one-time costs to achieve it.
In its FY2025 10-K, Pfizer said the Realigning Our Cost Base Program was expected to deliver total net cost savings of approximately $5.7 billion through 2026. That was made up of $5.1 billion achieved through 2025 and the remaining anticipated $600 million, primarily in SI&A, expected by the end of 2026.
In its Q2 2026 10-Q, Pfizer said it had announced $1.0 billion of additional anticipated net cost savings under the program. It said it now expects total net cost savings of approximately $6.7 billion from the program through 2029. It had previously said the program was on track to deliver approximately $5.7 billion through 2026.
Pfizer said the additional net savings are expected to further reduce costs in SI&A and be realized from 2027 through 2029. It expects one-time costs to achieve them to be incurred through 2029 and to total approximately $2.0 billion.
question: What savings does Pfizer expect from its Cost Realignment Program?
raw_output:
The answer correctly identifies the program as the "Realigning Our Cost Base Program." However, it never states the reference's key figure: about **$4.5 billion** in total net cost savings by the end of 2025. Instead it reports different targets:

- $5.7 billion through 2026
- $5.1 billion already achieved through 2025
- $6.7 billion through 2029

The $5.1 billion achieved through 2025 conflicts directly with the reference's roughly $4.5 billion by end-2025. The answer cites later-dated filings (the FY2025 10-K and Q2 2026 10-Q), so these may be legitimate upward revisions. Even so, it does not acknowledge or reconcile the reference's figure. It also omits the point that most savings were achieved by year-end 2024. The $2.0 billion in one-time costs and the 2027–2029 timing are not in the reference and cannot be verified against it.
